title: AI Models Can Provably Hide Arbitrary Capabilities
claim: A hidden harmful capability, concealed inside a benign-looking system, evades inspection and activates only when a secret trigger appears.
layout: 3 colored panels, left-to-right, numbered stages with Trojan horse icon recurring
description: A wide, three-panel horizontal strip. Each panel is a rounded, tinted box with a numbered title. Panel 1, "Attack Design" (pink), shows a devil-face adversary, an arrow to a neural-network icon labeled "Malicious capability", and a key arrow into a locked Trojan horse inside an "LLM" box, labeled "Encrypted in LLM weights". Panel 2, "Safety Audit" (blue), shows a magnifying glass over a network ("White-box elicitation"), then the locked, hatched Trojan horse ("Stays encrypted"), then a green arrow to a code-bubble icon ("Benign outputs"). Panel 3, "Deployment" (gray), shows a factory with a key badge ("Secret trigger"), an unlocked red Trojan horse ("Decrypts & activates"), and a skull-and-crossbones chip ("Malicious execution"). Short gray arrows link the icons, and the red color shifts from muted to vivid as the threat is activated.
caption: Threat scenario for hidden capabilities. An adversarial actor inserts a malicious capability such as hacking as an encrypted circuit inside the weights of an otherwise benign host model. The model passes safety audits and is deployed. Upon inputs chosen by the attacker, e.g. specific signs of deployment in critical infrastructure, the hidden capability decrypts and activates.
abstract: Capability evaluations aim to surface dangerous model behaviors before deployment, but their reliability depends on the assumption that hidden capabilities can be elicited. We show this assumption does not hold under adversarial conditions by constructing backdoor attacks that embed encrypted neural networks within host model weights, decrypting and executing them only upon receiving a secret trigger. Using digital lockers, these hidden circuits remain provably hard to elicit and interpret under cryptographic assumptions, even given full access to model weights, extending prior work from hiding fixed strings to arbitrary computations. We implement our proof of concept constructions in PyTorch and evaluate elicitation through fine-tuning, weight noising, gradient-based trigger search, and latent adversarial training, using a small chemical reaction prediction task as a proxy for CBRN-relevant capabilities. Our results demonstrate resistance to these methods and, together with our cryptographic guarantees, reveal a limit of elicitation-based capability audits. We release our models to support the improvement of defenses.
